# AGENTS.md

Guidance for any AI agent (Codex, Claude, or otherwise) that decides to use
`paperpush` to submit a manuscript to a venue - a journal, preprint server, or conference -
on a user's behalf.

## Skills: which one to use, and when

paperpush ships its workflows as agent skills (`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`). If
yours are installed, use the matching skill instead of working from this file
alone: it holds the same contract, step by step. If you can't load skills,
open the `SKILL.md` and follow it as written.

| Skill | What it does | Call it when the user... |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `paperpush-prepare-submission` | The whole flow: checks the login, finds or creates the `.sub`, runs autofill, runs validate, then (once the user confirms) runs submit. | asks to prepare, get ready, or submit a manuscript to a venue, and has not named a single step. **Start here when in doubt.** |
| `paperpush-autofill` | Reads the manuscript directory, writes `values.json`, and applies it with `paperpush autofill --engine manual`. Leaves `never` fields for the author. | wants a `.sub` filled from their files, and nothing else yet. |
| `paperpush-validate` | Runs `paperpush validate`, then does the checks that need a reader (lettering in raster figures, panel labels, free-text guideline rules, `.sub` vs manuscript) through `--ai-tasks` / `--ai-results`. Optionally saves the report. | asks whether a manuscript or `.sub` is ready, meets a venue's guidelines, or passes validation, or wants the AI checks or a saved report. |
| `paperpush-portal-debug` | Gets a stalled `paperpush submit` run past the failing step on the live page (`submit_page` / `submit_act` / `submit_resume`), logs every runner change it needs, and puts those changes into the runner with a test when working in a source checkout. Never sends the submission. | reports that `submit` is stuck, failed at a step, or hit a portal that changed. Also use it yourself whenever `submit_status` shows `recovery.paused`. |
| `paperpush-add-venue-validate` | Reads a venue's author guidelines and records them in `manuscript_requirements.json`, and its basic submission fields in `submission_forms.json`, through a venue file and `paperpush add-venue`. For an existing venue, re-reads the pages and updates what changed. | wants a venue that `validate` can check against, or wants a venue's guidelines, limits, or rules added or refreshed. *Contributor skill: needs a clone of the repo.* |
| `paperpush-add-venue` | Full `submit` support: a `Venue` class with Playwright `login()` / `submit()`, the portal's fields, a sample `.sub` with generated documents, unit tests, and a live run that stops before the final submit. For an existing runner, runs its tests and fixes what fails. Has the user create an account and run `paperpush login` rather than handing over a password. | wants to submit to a venue paperpush can't submit to yet, or reports that a venue's runner or tests are broken. Runs `paperpush-add-venue-validate` first if the venue has no guidelines entry yet. *Contributor skill: needs a clone of the repo.* |

The skills call each other where the steps overlap: `prepare-submission` runs
`autofill` and `validate`; `add-venue` runs `add-venue-validate`, and uses
`portal-debug` for a live step that stalls. Don't run the same step twice.

### Installing the skills

- **Claude Code**: `/plugin marketplace add pachterlab/paperpush`, then
  `/plugin install paperpush@paperpush`. Or, with paperpush installed,
  `paperpush install-skills` (`--all` adds the contributor skills,
  `--project .` installs into the current project only).
- **Codex**: `codex plugin marketplace add pachterlab/paperpush`, then
  `codex plugin add paperpush@paperpush`. Or `paperpush install-skills --agent codex`.
- **Any other agent**: `paperpush install-skills --dest <that agent's skills
  directory>`, or point it at `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
- **In a clone of this repo**, Claude Code already loads them from
  `.claude/skills/`, which links to `skills/`.

## The one rule: you are the extractor

`paperpush` splits submission into two layers:

- **You (the agent) propose values.** You read the manuscript files and decide
  what each submission field should contain.
- **The `paperpush` CLI writes and validates.** A deterministic core does
  all the writing, policy gating, path resolution, and validation, so you cannot
  overwrite a policy field or produce an invalid file.

**Do your own autofilling.** Read the manuscript yourself and hand the CLI a
`values.json`. Do **not** reach for `paperpush autofill --engine api` — that
path calls an LLM API (Anthropic, OpenAI, or Google) and needs that provider's
API key (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, or `GEMINI_API_KEY`). You already have
the manuscript in front of you; extract from it directly. Use `--engine api`
only if the user has explicitly set an API key and asked for it.

**Don't run `--web` or `paperpush web` yourself.** They serve a page in the
user's browser and keep running until Ctrl-C, so your command never returns.
Suggest them to a user who wants to fill in or review a `.sub` in a form, and
let the user run them in their own terminal.

## Before anything else: check the user is logged in

The pipeline ends in a real browser sign-in, and that sign-in is the one step you
cannot do for the user — it may need their password, ORCID, a CAPTCHA, or a
two-factor code. Check it **first**, before you read a single manuscript file, so
the user can log in while you work instead of discovering the blocker at the end:

```
paperpush login --list
```

It prints `Not logged in to any venues.` or a `Logged in to:` block with one
`<venue>: <who>` line per stored credential. If the target venue is not in that
list, stop and tell the user right away — in your very next message — to run the
login themselves in their terminal:

```
paperpush login <venue>
```

Say plainly that this opens a browser and is theirs to complete, and that you
will keep going in the meantime. Do not run `paperpush login` yourself, and do
not treat a missing login as a reason to skip the extraction work — do the
`.sub` creation, autofill, and validation regardless, then run
`paperpush login <venue> --check` before the submit step. `--check` signs in
headless with the stored credentials, so it also catches a password changed
since login; `--list` and `--status` only show that something is stored. On
exit 1, ask the user to run `paperpush login <venue>` again.

Some public submission systems do not have author accounts. If the target is
absent from `--list`, check it with `paperpush login <venue> --status` before
asking the user to sign in. A loginless venue reports that it does not require
login and exits successfully; proceed without credentials in that case.

(For a single venue, `paperpush login <venue> --status` gives the same answer;
`--list` is the one call that covers "am I logged in anywhere yet".)

**Connected over MCP instead of a shell?** `login_status` is this check, and
`login_status(venue=...)` is the per-venue form — it returns the exact
`login_command` to pass along when the venue is not signed in. Before
`submit`, call `login_status(venue=..., check=true)`, the MCP form of
`--check`: a `check.status` of `failed` or `timed_out` sets `logged_in` to false
and gives the `login_command`. The `login` tool
is the same guard in one call: it reports an existing login, and otherwise hands
back the command for the user to run, so the user's password never passes
through the conversation. (It does run the login itself when
`PAPERPUSH_USERNAME` and `PAPERPUSH_PASSWORD` are already set in the server's
environment.) Everything else in this document maps to a tool too —
`list_supported_venues`, `describe_venue` for the schema, `field_options`,
`create_subfile`, `read_subfile`, `autofill_subfile` (same `values.json` shape,
passed as the `values` argument), `validate_subfile`, `submit`, `submit_status`,
`submit_page`, `submit_act`, `submit_resume`, and `submit_close`. Pass **absolute paths**: the server has its own working
directory, so a relative path means something different to it than it does to
you.

`submit` is the one tool that does not finish its work before returning. The
wizard fills the form and then parks holding the browser open for the author, so
the tool hands back a `pid` as soon as the run has started: poll `submit_status`
for progress, tell the user to review and send the form themselves, and call
`submit_close` when they say they are done. It refuses to open a browser at all
unless the `.sub` validates and, when the portal requires authentication, the
venue already has a stored login — so run the login check above first.

**When a step fails, the run pauses for you instead of failing** (on every venue
with a submission runner; sign-in is never part of it). `submit_status` then
reports `recovery.paused` with what the script was trying to do, the step
it was on, and the error. Then:

1. `submit_page(pid)`: the page's accessibility snapshot plus a screenshot path.
2. `submit_act(pid, action, target, value)`: click, fill, select, check,
   upload, and so on, to make the page look the way the failed step should have
   left it. Target elements by role and name (`{"role": "button", "name":
   "Next"}`), by label, by text, or by CSS.
3. `submit_resume(pid, "resolved" | "retry" | "abort", note)`. `resolved`
   means the step is done and the script moves on to its next line, `retry`
   runs the step again, and `abort` fails the run. Say in `note` what had
   changed, because it is logged so the venue script can be fixed.

If a similar step already failed earlier in the run (upload row 2 after row
1), `recovery.paused` and `submit_page` include `earlier_fix`: the actions that
worked last time and the note. Adapt it (index, values) rather than copying it.
An identical failure that was fixed only by waiting or clicking a named button
is repeated by the run itself, without pausing.

**Never fix a run by editing paperpush's installed code.** A user who installed
with `pip` would lose the change on the next upgrade, and no one else would get it.
Fix the live page with the tools above. When steps needed recovery,
`submit_status` says so (`recovery.report`): once the author is done, call
`recovery_report(pid)` and show them the redacted draft (`title`, `body`).
Give them `issue_url` to file it themselves if they want the venue fixed for
everyone. Never open or submit it for them.

You cannot send the submission this way: clicks on `Submit` / `Approve`
controls, Enter key presses, and uploads of files the `.sub` does not name are
refused. A paused run you never resume gives up after 30 minutes. Pass
`expose_cdp=True` to `submit` only if you need to drive the browser with
another tool (`playwright-cli attach --cdp=<cdp_endpoint>`). That endpoint
bypasses these guardrails, so never use it to send the submission.

Don't add `paperpush submit --ai` yourself. It pays for an LLM API to do the
recovery that you can do through the tools above, so use it only if the user has
an API key set and asked for it, the same rule as `autofill --engine api`.

## Run the full pipeline, autofilling yourself

The whole flow — create the `.sub`, fill it from your values, validate, log in,
submit — runs from `scripts/paperpush_pipeline.py`. The autofill step
defaults to `--engine manual`, which applies the `values.json` **you** wrote. So
"run the full pipeline but do your own autofilling" is:

1. **Learn the fields.** Get the schema (roles + constraints) without needing a
   `.sub` to exist yet:

   ```
   paperpush schema <venue>
   ```

   Each field carries a `role`:
   - `extract`  — copy a value verbatim from the manuscript (title, abstract,
     author list, competing-interest / funding / data-availability statements,
     page/figure/table counts, a repo URL or accession printed in the paper).
   - `classify` — choose exactly one of the field's `options`, or answer
     `yes`/`no` for a boolean declaration. Use `medium` confidence at best so the
     value is flagged for the author.
   - `filemap`  — assign a file (or files) from the directory to the field.
   - `never`    — **do not fill.** Consent/attestations, license and payment
     choices, suggested/opposed reviewers, identifiers you'd have to invent
     (DOIs, manuscript IDs), and workflow flags. List these in `unfilled` with a
     one-line reason and move on.

2. **Read the files and write `values.json`.** Read the user-identified files
   directly (convert `.docx`/`.tex` to text first). Prefer a title page or
   LaTeX/Word source over a flattened PDF for author metadata. Then write:

   ```json
   {
     "fields": [
       {"id": "title", "value": "...", "confidence": "high", "source": "manuscript.pdf p.1"},
       {"id": "authors",
        "value": "Ada Lovelace | ada@example.edu | Example University |  | yes",
        "confidence": "medium", "source": "title_page.pdf"},
       {"id": "subject_category", "value": "Bioinformatics",
        "confidence": "medium", "source": "classified from abstract"},
       {"id": "manuscript_file", "value": "/abs/path/manuscript.pdf",
        "confidence": "high", "source": "directory"},
       {"id": "figure_files",
        "value": "/abs/path/figures/fig1.png | Figure 1\n/abs/path/figures/fig2.png | Figure 2",
        "confidence": "high", "source": "figures/"}
     ],
     "unfilled": [
       {"id": "license", "reason": "license is the author's policy choice"},
       {"id": "author_consent", "reason": "all authors must consent -- confirm yourself"}
     ]
   }
   ```

   Rules for the values:
   - `authors`: one line per author in the venue's column order, given in that
     field's `help` — usually `Name | email | affiliation | ORCID |
     corresponding` with exactly one corresponding author marked `yes`, but some
     venues reorder the columns and some (arXiv) take the name alone. Leave a
     subfield blank (keep the `|`) rather than inventing an email or ORCID.
   - `filemap`: use **absolute paths**; only the leading path segment is
     resolved, so extra columns (`| label`, or bioRxiv `| type | linktext`) are
     preserved as written.
   - `confidence`: `high` = copied verbatim / unambiguous file match; `medium` =
     inferred, reformatted, or a classification; `low` = a genuine guess. When
     unsure, lower the confidence rather than guessing high.
   - Never put a `never`-role field in `fields`; put it in `unfilled`.

3. **Run the pipeline** with your values (use absolute paths throughout):

   ```
   python scripts/paperpush_pipeline.py <venue> \
       -p /abs/path/to/manuscript-dir \
       --values /abs/path/to/values.json
   ```

   This runs `subfile` → `autofill --engine manual` (applying your values) →
   `validate` → `login` → `submit`, stopping at the first failure. The `login`
   step is interactive, so it is the user's to complete in their terminal — if
   the pre-flight check above showed them logged out, make sure they have run
   `paperpush login <venue>` before you kick off the pipeline. The submit
   step opens the portal headed and stops before the final click so the user can
   review. Add `--headless`, `--force`, etc. as the user needs (see `--help`).
   `--orcid` signs in with the user's ORCID iD and ORCID password instead of a
   venue account — offer it only if the user says that is how they sign in. It
   works for bioRxiv, medRxiv, arXiv, the Editorial Manager journals (Cell
   family and PLOS Computational Biology), BMC Bioinformatics, and Genome
   Biology; other venues report that the flow is not recorded yet, and
   conference portals refuse it.

If you prefer to drive the steps yourself instead of the pipeline script, the
autofill step alone is:

```
paperpush autofill <venue>.sub -p <manuscript-dir> --engine manual --values values.json
```

(Add `--dry-run` to preview without writing. `-p` accepts several directories
and/or documents -- `.tex`, `.doc`, `.docx`, `.odt`, `.rtf`, `.txt`, `.md`, `.rst`,
`.pdf` -- e.g. `-p ms/ figures/ cover_letter.docx`; it stops at the next flag or
the first `.sub` file, and may be repeated.)

## The manuscript itself is checked too

`validate` (and the pipeline's validate step) measures the uploaded files
against the venue's author guidelines -- word/page limits for the selected
article type, required sections and statements, title-page items, figure
resolution and dimensions, reference count, file formats and sizes. A LaTeX
manuscript is compiled with `latexmk`/`pdflatex` for its page count when a
toolchain is installed. To see the rules before you fill anything, run
`paperpush requirements <venue>` (or read `manuscript_requirements` in the
MCP `describe_venue` result), and pick the article type in `values.json`
accordingly, since it selects which limits apply. The same pass checks the page
layout (template, margins, font, spacing, line/page numbers, spelling variant),
the figures (resolution, lettering size and typeface, panel labels -- attached
files, or the figures embedded in the manuscript when none are attached), that
figures, tables, and figure panels are cited in order, and that the title, abstract, authors,
keywords, and statements in the `.sub` match the manuscript; that the abstract
cites no references (and is structured when the venue asks), the manuscript
gives a contact e-mail, every reference is cited, and self-citations are not
excessive; and proofreads the prose mechanically (double spaces, repeated
words, punctuation spacing, unbalanced brackets and quotes, common
misspellings, repetitive word choice). Warnings from this
pass are heuristics over extracted text and images: relay them to the user as
things to confirm, not as blockers. `--dont-check-manuscript` skips the pass.

## The report, and the checks you run yourself

`validate` reports every check as passed, failed, warning, could not run, needs
AI, not implemented, or not applicable (MCP: `checks` in the `validate_subfile`
result). `-o` saves the report (PDF by default; `.html`/`.md`/`.txt` by
extension); `--colorblind` is the colour-blind-friendly palette.
When the venue lets the initial submission be in any format
(`manuscript.initial_submission_any_format`), the report opens with that rule
(MCP: `initial_submission_rule`); `--initial-submission` (MCP:
`initial_submission=true`) reports every error as a warning for a first
submission. Use it only when the author says this is an initial submission.

Checks that need a reader's judgement -- lettering in raster figures, a postal
address on the title page, tables pasted as images, the venue's free-text
guideline rules, whether each `.sub` field means what the manuscript says --
come back as **needs AI**. Do them yourself rather than asking the user for an
API key:

1. `paperpush validate <abs .sub> --ai-tasks <scratch>/tasks.json` (MCP:
   `validation_ai_tasks`). Each task has an `id`, `instructions`, and the
   `files` to read.
2. Read the files and judge each task: `pass`, `fail` (say exactly what and
   where), `unclear`, or `not_applicable`. Figure tasks give the minimum
   lettering size as a fraction of the image width; measure against it.
3. Write `{"results": [{"id", "status", "details", "evidence"}]}` and run
   `paperpush validate <abs .sub> --ai-results <that file>` (MCP:
   `validate_subfile(ai_results=[...])`). Add `--ai-only` (MCP:
   `ai_only=True`) to report just the AI checks, e.g. when re-checking them.

An AI `fail` is a warning, never a blocking error; do not mark a task `pass`
you could not verify. With an API key, `paperpush validate --ai` does the same
through the provider's API. The Claude skill `paperpush-validate` walks
through these steps.

## Double-blind venues are checked for identifying information

Venues marked `"anonymous": true` in `venues.json` (ICLR, AAAI) get an
anonymity pass on every `validate`; `paperpush validate --anonymous` (MCP:
`validate_subfile(anonymous=true)`) runs it for any other venue. It searches the
attached files and the `.sub`'s text fields for the authors' names, emails,
ORCID/OpenReview IDs and affiliations (from the author list), author metadata
(PDF, Office, EXIF), home-directory paths, an acknowledgments section, and
camera-ready LaTeX switches, and it fetches every linked
anonymous.4open.science repository and scans that too, including an expired or
missing mirror. Warnings start with `anonymity:`; relay each one to the user,
since a leak can get a paper desk-rejected.

## Other desk-reject checks validate runs

- **Hidden text / prompt injection** (every venue; `--dont-check-hidden-text`
  skips it). White, invisible, microscopic, or off-page text in the PDF,
  LaTeX, or Word uploads. Hidden text that instructs an AI reviewer is an
  **error**. Tell the user exactly what was found and where, and never add such
  text yourself. Reading PDFs needs the optional `validate` extra. If validate warns
  "PDF checks skipped … need pdfminer.six", tell the user to run
  `pip install 'paperpush[validate]'`, because the checks did not run.
- **Uncleaned arXiv LaTeX source** (arXiv and venues that submit through it;
  part of the sensitive-info scan). If validate warns that the source still has
  comments or unneeded files, offer `paperpush validate --arxiv-latex-cleaner`:
  it writes cleaned copies next to the originals (`paper_arXiv/`,
  `source_arXiv.zip`) and validates those. It does not edit the .sub, so point
  the upload fields at the cleaned copies before submitting. Needs
  `pip install 'paperpush[validate]'`.
- **Modified template** (venues whose `manuscript_requirements.json` entry has
  `manuscript.template_layout`, e.g. ICLR). The manuscript PDF's margins, body
  font, line spacing, running head, and review line numbers are measured
  against the official template, and attached LaTeX source is read for
  `geometry`, `\linespread`, text-block `\setlength`s, and heavy negative
  `\vspace`. Warnings start with `template:`. Changing the paper's layout is the
  author's call: report these to the user rather than editing their source.
- **OpenReview profiles** (OpenReview venues: ICLR, AAAI;
  `--dont-check-openreview-profiles` skips it). Each author is looked up
  through the OpenReview API using the stored `paperpush login`. Reported:
  missing, ambiguous, or inactive profiles, name or email-suffix mismatches, no
  current position, and reviewers without DBLP or expertise. Messages start
  with `openreview:`. Without a stored login the check is skipped with a note;
  that is another reason to have the user log in first. Profile fixes happen on
  openreview.net and are the user's to make.

## After it runs, tell the user what's left

`paperpush` deliberately leaves the `never` fields blank. Spell out for the
user exactly what remains: the `never` fields (each with its `unfilled` reason),
any review-flagged values to confirm, and any remaining validation errors (the
file will not submit until those are resolved).

## Claude Code note

If you are Claude Code, use the skills in
[Skills: which one to use, and when](#skills-which-one-to-use-and-when) above.
They hold this same contract.
